title: Pros and Cons of Offering Referral Bonuses
summary: Considering offering referral bonuses to employees? We've created a pros and cons list for you to consider.
body_markdown:
43% of new frontline hires leave within 90 days, according to the


[2025 Fountain Frontline Report](https://ebook.fountain.com/frontline-report-2025) , so a referral bonus paid on a hire who quits in week six rewards a placement that didn’t last. Referred hires tend to


[stay longer](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25920) , and a referral program can cut replacement hiring and labor costs.


Against that, referrals can narrow who gets hired, large rewards invite weak submissions, and botched payouts turn a perk into a grievance. Most of that traces to program design, covered below alongside amount, timing, and policy.


## What is an employee referral bonus?


An employee referral bonus is a reward, usually cash, that an employer pays a current worker for recommending a candidate who is then hired, once the referred person reaches a defined point in the hiring process. Payroll typically treats it as taxable pay to the referrer, and it differs from a sign-on bonus, which goes to the new hire.


It is one piece of a referral program, which also covers how workers share openings, how referrals get tracked, and the written rules. Money still matters: the grocery-chain trial covered below found its


[information-only arm](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25920/w25920.pdf) produced no referrals.


What counts as a “successful” referral shapes everything below. Employers define it as the hire, Day 1, or a retention milestone such as 30, 60, or 90 days.


## Pros of offering employee referral bonuses


Employee referral bonuses can lower attrition and labor costs, improve retention, and reach candidates job boards miss, according to a randomized trial across 238 stores at a European grocery chain (


[NBER Working Paper 25920](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25920) , later published in the Journal of Political Economy).


- **Referred hires tend to leave less often.** They showed


[45% lower attrition](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25920/w25920.pdf) than observably similar non-referrals over the 13-month study, so fewer replacement hires.


- **A program improves retention across the whole store.**[Attrition fell 15%](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25920) in stores with a referral program, even those where no one made a referral, and labor costs fell significantly.


- **Referrals reach local and passive candidates that job boards miss.** A cook’s cousin who isn’t job hunting may never see a sponsored posting but will likely open a text with a link.


- **Bonuses can target the shifts and sites that are hardest to fill.** North Carolina’s state program


[limits referral bonuses to classifications](https://oshr.nc.gov/documents/employee-referral-bonus-pilot-program-policy/open) it deems hard to fill, and an employer can aim the same lever at an overnight shift or a hard-to-staff site.


Most of the payoff comes from retention, not volume.


## Cons of offering employee referral bonuses


Employee referral bonuses can reinforce workforce homogeneity, create perceived favoritism, attract weak submissions, cause payout disputes, and overconcentrate recruiting in one channel.


- **Referral hiring can mirror the workforce you already have.** The EEOC’s


[Compliance Manual](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/section-15-race-and-color-discrimination) says word-of-mouth recruiting in a non-diverse workforce “is a barrier to equal employment opportunity if it does not create applicant pools that reflect the diversity in the qualified labor market.” Fountain’s look at whether


[diversity gaps start in sourcing or screening](https://www.fountain.com/posts/diversity-hiring-sourcing-or-screening-problem) shows where to check.


- **Referred candidates can appear to get an easier path.** When a hiring manager knows who referred a candidate, others can suspect an advantage, real or not.


- **Large bonuses can pull in weak submissions.** Larger bonuses raise referral quantity


[but lower quality](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25920/w25920.pdf) , as workers become “willing to refer less qualified friends because the financial reward is higher.”


- **Duplicate claims and late payouts can turn a perk into a grievance.** A timestamped


[first-submission rule](https://careers.lluh.org/benefits/employee-referral-program) settles duplicates, and a payout that arrives late costs you the referrer’s trust.


- **Referrals can’t carry a high-volume pipeline alone.** In the grocery trial, even the largest bonus produced referrals for


[only 5% of hires](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25920/w25920.pdf) .


Bonus size, payout timing, eligibility, and screening rules can reduce each of these problems.


## How much should a referral bonus be?


The right amount depends on the role, the urgency, and what filling it another way would cost, not on an industry average. The ceiling is the alternative:


[SHRM’s 2025 benchmarking](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) put the average nonexecutive cost-per-hire at $5,475.


Frontline programs can pay one flat amount for any eligible role, the simplest structure to explain on a break-room poster, or use tiers by hiring difficulty and surges for a shortage or a season.


A bigger bonus isn’t automatically a better one. In


[the grocery-chain trial](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25920/w25920.pdf) , the program’s effect on attrition showed no clear relation to bonus size, while more money brought more names and weaker ones.

Non-cash rewards usually don’t escape payroll either: IRS


[Publication 15-B](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15b) (2026 edition) says cash equivalents such as gift cards, “no matter how little,” are never excludable as a de minimis benefit, so a $100 gift card typically shows up as $100 of taxable pay.


Confirm with payroll or counsel and ask your crews what they’d value before setting the amount.


## When should referral bonuses be paid?


Pay at a defined milestone, typically 45 to 90 days after the hire starts. In WorldatWork’s 2021 survey, 1.5 to 3 months was


[the most common window](https://worldatwork.org/media/CDN/dist/CDN2/documents/pdf/resources/research/WAW1021_Survey_KF_Bonus-Programs-and-Practices_FNL.pdf) before a referrer received the full bonus. A Day 1 payout confirms someone showed up, while a 90-day payout confirms the placement held, the outcome you were buying.


Day 1 rewards the referral quickly, but a pending bonus keeps the referrer involved: referrals that outperform other hires do so,


[Peter Cappelli wrote in SHRM](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/viewpoint-approach-to-hiring-wrong) , because their referrers “look after them and essentially onboard them.” A split payout gets both: part on Day 1 and the rest at 90 days.


SHRM’s


[Jessica Miller-Merrell](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-to-create-employee-referral-program) calls a 90- or 120-day retention bonus on top of a first-day bonus “the secret sauce for a robust referral program.”


Most programs document what happens when someone leaves early. North Carolina’s Department of Adult Correction, for one,


[states in its FAQ](https://www.dac.nc.gov/employee-referral-bonus-faq) that the referrer must be employed when each payment is made. Rules on withholding after separation vary by state, so confirm the wording with employment counsel.


When HR can tell a referrer that their friend has finished onboarding and the 90-day payment is on track, the wait feels like a schedule.


## What to include in a referral bonus policy


A written policy can help prevent the cons above, and many employers put one in place before the first referral arrives. A practical policy covers five points:


1. **Spell out who’s eligible, who’s excluded, and which roles qualify.** Policies commonly exclude hiring managers, selection-team members, and anyone with a direct reporting relationship to the candidate, and some also exclude


[HR staff](https://www.lakecountyca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/7639/Employee-Referral-Program) . Some programs cover every opening, while others limit bonuses to hard-to-fill roles.


2. **Set the timing rules for credit.** Some programs require the referral to be recorded before the candidate applies, and duplicates go to the first submission.


3. **Decide whether nonemployees can refer.** Some programs


[accept nonemployee referrals](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/6-tips-effective-employee-referral-programs) , such as customers or clients, and payroll or a tax adviser can confirm reporting before paying a nonemployee.


4. **Give every referred candidate the same structured evaluation.** Referred applicants complete the same screening, interview, and background steps, which addresses favoritism, and


[broad outreach](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/eeoc-enforcement-guidance-national-origin-discrimination) can widen the applicant pool, the concern behind the EEOC’s word-of-mouth guidance.


5. **State the tax treatment.**[The IRS’s Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15) (2026 edition) covers bonuses as supplemental wages in Section 7, and payroll can confirm how withholding applies to referral bonuses.


A one-page policy covering those five points gives employment counsel a draft to review. Overtime is one question for them: the DOL’s


[Fact Sheet #56C](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/56c-bonuses) lists referral bonuses as potentially excludable from the regular rate, case by case.


## How to run a referral bonus program for frontline teams


Don’t let a frontline referral program live only in email. Workers who skip company email will tap a


[text link or scan a QR code](https://www.fountain.com/posts/source-candidates-without-job-board-fees) on the break-room wall, and


[requiring a resume at submission](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-to-get-people-to-use-employee-referral-program) discourages participation. Referrers who hear nothing back are


[unlikely to refer again](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-to-get-people-to-use-employee-referral-program) , so close the loop on every referral. Rules and payout timing also need to be identical across locations, since a bonus that pays at 30 days in one district and 90 in another is a grievance waiting for a group chat.


The metric to track is retained hires at 90 days by source and location, the


[source-of-hire and retention view](https://www.fountain.com/posts/recruitment-funnel) a frontline funnel needs. A raw referral count rewards volume, and in the grocery-chain trial higher volume came with lower quality.

## Frequently asked questions about employee referral bonuses


### What happens when two employees refer the same candidate?


A clear policy can use the first referral received as the tie-breaker. Other programs, such as North Carolina’s,


[split the bonus pro rata](https://oshr.nc.gov/documents/employee-referral-bonus-pilot-program-policy/open) when a candidate names more than one referrer.


### Should you still pay if the new hire quits?


It depends on the policy’s payment milestone and on state law. With a Day 1 trigger, the written policy sets whether the bonus is payable once the person started. With a 90-day trigger and a hire who left at day 60, some programs, such as North Carolina’s, stop remaining payments, and under a split structure the policy states whether the first installment stays. Confirm the wording with employment counsel.


### Can employees earn a bonus for referring family members?


It depends on the employer’s written policy. Bowdoin College’s


[family definition](https://www.bowdoin.edu/hr/benefits-perks/other-benefits/employee-referral-bonus-program.html) for excluded referrals runs from spouses and partners to grandchildren, while Lake County, California


[allows family referrals](https://www.lakecountyca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/7639/Employee-Referral-Program) .
